title: Exercise form fundamentals
chunks: Good form means moving the weight through a controlled, full range of motion with the target muscle doing the work and your body braced and stable. It both maximizes the stimulus to the muscle and reduces injury risk. Form is the foundation that lets you load progressively for years.

Control the weight in both directions. Lower under control (about 1–3 seconds) rather than dropping it, and avoid bouncing or using momentum. The lowering (eccentric) portion is a major driver of muscle growth, so rushing it leaves results on the table.

Use a full range of motion that you can control — a deep stretch under load and a full contraction. Training through a longer range, especially the stretched position, tends to build more muscle than short, partial reps. Only shorten range if a position causes pain.

Brace your core and keep a stable, neutral spine on standing and compound lifts. A tight midsection protects your back and gives you a solid base to press or pull from. Think 'proud chest, braced trunk' on squats, deadlifts, rows, and presses.

Pick weights you can control with good technique. If you have to heave, swing, or contort to move a load, it is too heavy — drop the weight, own the movement, and progress from there. Ego lifting trades long-term progress and joint health for a heavier-looking set.

Learn the basic movement patterns: a squat, a hinge (like a Romanian deadlift), a horizontal and vertical push, a horizontal and vertical pull, and a carry. Most effective programs are built from these patterns plus isolation work for specific muscles.

If a movement causes sharp or joint pain (not normal muscular effort), stop and reassess — adjust the setup, reduce the load, or choose a variation that feels better. For persistent or significant pain, see a qualified physiotherapist or doctor rather than training through it.
